report:
## Conclusion

The claim that CLA supplements reduce abdominal fat is **weakly supported and likely overstated**. Multiple randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses show CLA can produce small, statistically significant reductions in body fat mass, and some individual trials (e.g., a 12-week RCT in overweight/obese women) found modest decreases in visceral, android, and total fat via imaging (https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/12/6/1811). Early studies also reported reduced abdominal adipose tissue using waist/sagittal diameter measures (https://www.nature.com/articles/0801659).

However, larger and more rigorous evidence is less convincing. A comprehensive meta-analysis of human trials found CLA's fat-reducing effect, while statistically detectable, was very small (roughly 0.05–0.1 kg/week) and of uncertain clinical significance (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0002916523280557). A 2011 systematic review/meta-analysis of long-term CLA trials in overweight/obese adults confirmed modest reductions in fat mass with corresponding preservation of lean mass, but effects were inconsistent across studies (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21990002/). A more recent (2023) dose-response meta-analysis concluded that CLA produced only small improvements in anthropometric measures, and that high-quality studies failed to demonstrate a genuine body-fat-lowering effect, casting doubt on earlier positive findings (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/effects-of-conjugated-linoleic-acid-supplementation-on-anthropometrics-and-body-composition-indices-in-adults-a-systematic-review-and-doseresponse-metaanalysis/A3F12F07BB3118D4F757D901C6E1E366).

**Bottom line:** CLA supplementation may yield trivial, inconsistent reductions in abdominal/visceral fat, but effects are not robust, clinically meaningful, or reliably targeted at abdominal fat specifically. It should not be relied upon as an effective fat-loss strategy; diet and exercise remain far more effective.
